faq.a: It is a disc of two metals bonded together. When heated, one expands more than the other, so the disc bends, and at a set temperature it snaps suddenly into a new shape.
asks: How does a bimetallic strip work?

faq.q: What clicks when a kettle turns off?
faq.a: The click is the bimetal disc snapping from one curve to the other, which pushes the switch open and cuts the electricity.

faq.q: Why does a kettle have a steam tube?
faq.a: Steam only appears in large amounts once the water is boiling. Sending it to the bimetal disc makes the kettle switch off at the right moment.
asks: How does a kettle know the water is boiling?

faq.q: What happens if you switch on an empty kettle?
faq.a: The element heats up very fast. A second safety disc under the element snaps and cuts the power before it can overheat or melt.

faq.q: Why does a kettle not switch off if the lid is open?
faq.a: With the lid open, the steam escapes out of the top instead of going down the tube to the switch, so the disc does not get hot enough.
asks: Why does my kettle keep boiling with the lid off?

facts: The Russell Hobbs K1 of 1955 is often described as the first automatic electric kettle, using a bimetallic strip heated by steam.
A bimetal disc snaps between two shapes because its two metals expand by different amounts when heated.
